Terminology-server expansions and official cross-version ConceptMaps were not available for external terminology.hl7.org value sets such as plan-definition-type, action-type, jurisdiction, and goal-priority.

scope.scopeNotesMd: This report compares the base R4 `PlanDefinition` StructureDefinition with the R6 ballot `PlanDefinition` StructureDefinition and focuses on local PlanDefinition element, binding, constraint, and representability changes. Search parameters, operations such as `$apply`, profiles such as shareable/computable PlanDefinition, examples, and datatype-internal changes are outside this artifact report except when needed to explain a local PlanDefinition field. Inherited-only changes from `Element`, `BackboneElement`, `Resource`, and `DomainResource` are excluded from `findings[]`.
outOfScope: Inherited/base-artifact changes from Element, BackboneElement, Resource, and DomainResource, including inherited modifierExtension summary-flag differences and inherited ele-1 wording changes.
R4/R6 OperationDefinition changes for PlanDefinition-apply and PlanDefinition-data-requirements.
Profiles derived from PlanDefinition, including shareableplandefinition, computableplandefinition, and cdshooksserviceplandefinition.
Internal breaking changes in referenced datatypes such as DataRequirement, RelatedArtifact, CodeableReference, RelativeTime, ContactDetail, TriggerDefinition, Expression, and UsageContext.
Terminology changes not present in the local core package or requiring terminology server expansion.

narrativeReportMd:
# PlanDefinition R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
R6 keeps the same `PlanDefinition` resource identity, but local element changes introduce several hard R4-to-R6 breaks and substantial R6-to-R4 representability risk. The highest-impact breaks are the `action.input`/`action.output` wrapper change, `relatedAction.actionId` to `targetId`, removal of `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod`, narrowing `action.code` to one repetition, and changed participant-type terminology/modeling.

## Scope
The analysis used the local R4 and R6 core package StructureDefinitions, package indexes, package metadata, and relevant local ValueSet/CodeSystem files. It excludes inherited base-artifact changes and separate PlanDefinition operations, search parameters, profiles, and datatype-internal changes.

## Main migration themes
PlanDefinition action orchestration changed from a simpler R4 shape to a richer R6 shape. Existing R4 action data requirements and related-action links need explicit structural transforms. R6 also adds new representational capacity for actors, data-flow links, relative timing, additional subject/definition targets, and action metadata that cannot be round-tripped into base R4 without extensions or loss.

## Highest-impact findings
The most direct validation breaks are `PlanDefinition:TYPE_DOMAIN:PlanDefinition.action.input-output:6b7e21`, `PlanDefinition:ELEMENT_PRESENCE_OR_IDENTITY:PlanDefinition.action.relatedAction:0a84ce`, `PlanDefinition:CARDINALITY:PlanDefinition.action.code:4dbf19`, `PlanDefinition:TYPE_DOMAIN:PlanDefinition.action.timing:38e58f`, and `PlanDefinition:TERMINOLOGY_BINDING:PlanDefinition.action.participant:bc41d0`.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is most important where automated transforms may lose semantics: choosing one `action.code` from multiple R4 concepts, converting absolute/period timing to R6 `Timing`, mapping participant-type code changes, and deciding how to preserve R6-only actor/data-flow/subject semantics in R4.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Some breaks could have been softened with deprecated aliases, retained choice types, warning invariants, or extensions. Other changes are mostly the expected cost of adding R6 expressivity that R4 did not model.

## Follow-up analysis
Datatype reports for `DataRequirement`, `RelativeTime`, `CodeableReference`, and `RelatedArtifact`, plus terminology expansion/ConceptMap review, would improve migration confidence.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: PlanDefinition has real local R4-to-R6 breaks, concentrated in action data requirements, related-action links, timing choices, action code cardinality, and participant terminology/modeling. The largest migration concerns are structural rewrites of action inputs/outputs, temporal/action-link semantics, and R6-only actor/subject/definition expressivity. The main uncertainty is terminology and rationale because official diffs, narrative ballot notes, expansions, and ConceptMaps were not available locally.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration should treat `PlanDefinition.action` as the center of risk. R4 data requirements must be wrapped under `requirement`; `relatedAction.actionId` must be renamed to `targetId`; `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod` need conversion to allowed R6 timing forms; repeated `action.code` values need consolidation or extension mapping; and participant codes/actors need terminology-aware conversion. Down-conversion from R6 to R4 requires an explicit policy for R6-only fields rather than silent dropping.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for structural, cardinality, type, and local CodeSystem findings because they are directly visible in the supplied R4 and R6 StructureDefinitions and package terminology files. Confidence is medium for exact terminology migration intent and prevalence because no official diff, narrative ballot discussion, terminology-server expansion, or ConceptMap was available.

findings.title: action.input and action.output changed from direct DataRequirement arrays to wrapper backbone elements

affectedLocation.newElementId: PlanDefinition.action.input; PlanDefinition.action.input.requirement; PlanDefinition.action.input.relatedData; PlanDefinition.action.output; PlanDefinition.action.output.requirement; PlanDefinition.action.output.relatedData

oldState.summary: Each action input or output item was a DataRequirement directly.
oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, `PlanDefinition.action.input` and `.output` are repeatable `DataRequirement` elements. DataRequirement fields such as `type`, `profile`, `codeFilter`, and `dateFilter` appear directly inside each `input[]` or `output[]` item.

newState.summary: Each item is now a BackboneElement with `requirement` or `relatedData`.

constraints.human: Input data elements must have a requirement or a relatedData, but not both
Output data element must have a requirement or a relatedData, but not both

newState.narrativeMd: In R6, `input[]` and `output[]` are wrapper backbone elements. A DataRequirement is nested under `requirement`; alternatively, `relatedData` can point to another input/output element. R6 also allows a human-readable `title` for the data-flow item.

facts.newValue: Exactly one of requirement or relatedData is required when an input/output backbone item is present.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The element names and definitions are preserved as action data inputs/outputs, but the representation changed by inserting a wrapper around the former DataRequirement content.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct JSON shape break. An R4 instance with `action.input[0].type` or `action.output[0].type` places DataRequirement properties at a location where R6 permits only the wrapper's children. Conversely, R6 `relatedData` and `title` have no R4 location, and R6 wrapper items must satisfy the new XOR constraint.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Data requirements often drive CDS prefetch, $data-requirements output, and execution orchestration. Mis-migration can change what data a plan is thought to consume or produce.

justification.inferredGoal: Support explicit data-flow labels and references between inputs and outputs while retaining DataRequirement as a nested requirement.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 direct DataRequirement arrays and add separate optional data-flow wrapper fields for titled or related-data items.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal is reasonable: `title`, `requirement`, `relatedData`, and the XOR invariants make action data flow more explicit than R4 direct `DataRequirement` arrays. A less-breaking base design exists, but it is only partial because preserving the old array while adding a richer wrapper would leave two same-resource representations for action inputs and outputs. That long-term duplication and validation ambiguity make the breaking wrapper design probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would keep `action.input` and `action.output` as repeatable `DataRequirement` elements and add new optional wrapper or sibling elements for titled/related data-flow entries. Existing R4 instances would continue to validate, but R6 receivers would have to support both direct requirements and wrapper entries, define conflict and precedence rules, and accept that the legacy representation may persist indefinitely.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old JSON but creates duplicate input/output representations and forces processors to reconcile direct requirements with wrapper or relatedData items.

evidence.detail: R4 action.input type is DataRequirement.
R4 action.output type is DataRequirement.
R6 action.input type is BackboneElement.
R6 nests the DataRequirement under input.requirement.
R6 requires exactly one of requirement or relatedData for an input item.
R6 requires exactly one of requirement or relatedData for an output item.

examples.examplesMd: The fragments are illustrative and focus on the changed location of DataRequirement content. A complete PlanDefinition may need additional business content.

findings.narrativeMd: `action.input` and `action.output` are the largest local representation break. R4 data requirements are no longer stored directly at those paths; R6 inserts a backbone wrapper and moves the former DataRequirement under `requirement`. Existing parsers, FHIRPath, JSON transforms, and generated model classes that read `action.input.type` or `action.output.profile` must be updated to look under `requirement` and to handle `relatedData` items that do not carry a DataRequirement at all.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances containing direct DataRequirement fields under `action.input[]` or `action.output[]` can become R6-invalid because those fields are not defined on the R6 wrapper. Valid R6 instances using `relatedData` are not cleanly representable in R4. R6 wrapper items with both `requirement` and `relatedData`, or neither, fail new error-level invariants.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Transform each R4 input/output DataRequirement into an R6 wrapper item with `requirement` containing the original DataRequirement. Preserve ordering. If migrating R6 back to R4, unwrap `requirement` losslessly but flag `title` and `relatedData` for extension mapping or manual review. Add tests for direct requirements, related-data links, and invalid items containing both alternatives.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 design likely needed an explicit wrapper to model data-flow labels and references. A backward-compatible alternative would have kept the R4 direct DataRequirement element and added optional extensions, but that would make core validation of the new relationship semantics difficult and less discoverable.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 put each action input/output DataRequirement directly under `action.input[]` or `action.output[]`; R6 changes those entries into backbone wrappers that carry either `requirement` or `relatedData`. That is a real wire-format and generated-model break for any converter, validator, or CDS prefetch logic reading `input.type` directly. The R6 goal is also concrete: a wrapper is the natural way to name data-flow items and express related-data links without pretending every item is itself a DataRequirement. The migration from R4 to R6 is mechanical for ordinary requirements, while R6-only `relatedData` needs explicit reverse-conversion policy.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.input` and `.output` are 0..* `DataRequirement`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.input` and `.output` are 0..* `BackboneElement` with nested `requirement` DataRequirement and `relatedData` id.
R6 constraints `pld-0` and `pld-1` require exactly one of `requirement` or `relatedData` on present wrapper entries.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 PlanDefinition is FMM 2/trial-use, so I treated maturity as neutral: the hard break matters, but the content does not have normative-level stability pressure.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: direct R4 DataRequirement properties at `action.input[]` or `action.output[]` are not R6 wrapper children; R6-to-R4 loss also exists for `title` and `relatedData`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial: R6 could have kept direct DataRequirement arrays and added separate sibling/wrapper elements for titled or related data, but that would create two same-purpose input/output representations and conflict rules. The wrapper design is disruptive but proportionate.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high impact and partial-alternative assessment; the break is real, but I would not escalate it to Revisit because the less-breaking design has material duplicate-representation costs.

findings.title: relatedAction.actionId was replaced by targetId and R6 added endRelationship

oldState.summary: R4 used required `actionId` of primitive type id.
oldState.narrativeMd: Each R4 relatedAction identifies the related action with required `actionId`. The value is constrained as an `id` primitive.

newState.summary: R6 uses required `targetId` of type string and adds optional `endRelationship`.

constraints.human: targetId should reference the id of an action

newState.narrativeMd: R6 renames the pointer to `targetId`, widens the primitive from `id` to `string`, and adds `endRelationship` to state the relationship of this action's end to the target action.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The old and new elements occupy the same parent, have the same required cardinality, and both identify the target related action.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Without a rename transform, an R4 relatedAction with `actionId` is missing the required R6 `targetId` and contains an unknown R6 element. R6 content using `endRelationship` loses timing semantics when represented in R4.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Related actions encode temporal orchestration. Losing or misreading the target or end relationship can change action ordering.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the related action is a target and allow both start and end relationship semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the R4 `actionId` wire name, widen or clarify its definition as the target action id, and add optional `endRelationship`.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Clarifying that the referenced action is a target and adding `endRelationship` are reasonable goals, but renaming the required wire element from `actionId` to `targetId` was not necessary to meet them. The `id` to `string` type change is a widening for R4 values, and `endRelationship` is additive. Keeping the old name with a clearer definition would preserve nearly all R4 instances with low long-term cost, so this break was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Base R6 could have kept `relatedAction.actionId` as the required element, defined it as the id of the target related action, widened the primitive type if needed, and added `endRelationship`. This avoids the conflict risk of having both `actionId` and `targetId`; the main downside is living with the older, less precise name.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Leaves a less-clear legacy name, but avoids duplicate target fields and preserves R4 instances while still supporting the R6 end-relationship semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 has required actionId of type id.
R6 has required targetId of type string.
R6 adds endRelationship with required binding to action-relationship-type.
R6 adds a warning that targetId should reference an action id.

examples.examplesMd: The key R4-to-R6 transform is renaming `actionId` to `targetId`. R6 `endRelationship` has no R4 peer.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 changes the required identifier inside each related action. This is a hard parser and validator issue because the old required name is not accepted as the new required name. R6 also adds the ability to describe the relationship of the end of an action, which can materially affect scheduling semantics and cannot be preserved by a simple R4 field rename.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `relatedAction.actionId` can be R6-invalid because `targetId` is absent. A strict R6 parser may also reject the unknown `actionId` member. R6 instances with `endRelationship` can only be represented in R4 by dropping, extending, or otherwise externalizing that end-bound timing detail.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Rename `actionId` to `targetId` during R4-to-R6 conversion and validate that the target references an action `id`. For R6-to-R4, rename `targetId` back to `actionId` only when the value is a valid R4 `id`, and preserve `endRelationship` in an extension or manual migration note.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The semantic addition is understandable, but the field rename could have been made less disruptive through a deprecated alias or transitional conversion rule. The main tradeoff is avoiding two competing target fields that could conflict.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The required related-action pointer was renamed from `actionId` to `targetId`. An R4 instance with `relatedAction.actionId` fails to populate the required R6 field even though the semantic role is essentially the same target action reference. The `id` to `string` type change is not a narrowing for normal R4 ids, and adding `endRelationship` is independently useful, so the hard break is driven mostly by a wire-name cleanup.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.relatedAction.actionId` is 1..1 `id`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.relatedAction.targetId` is 1..1 `string`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.relatedAction.endRelationship` is an added optional element.
R6 warning `pld-4` checks that `targetId` references an action id.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral, but it does not excuse a required element rename when the old name could plausibly have been retained.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 `actionId` is unknown to the R6 shape and leaves required `targetId` absent; R6-to-R4 loss applies only to the added `endRelationship`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes: keep `actionId` as the required wire name, clarify its definition as the target action id, widen its primitive type if needed, and add `endRelationship`. The tradeoff is living with a less precise legacy name, not a substantive modeling conflict.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing high-impact and less-breaking-alternative-available assessment; this looks like a low-cost avoidable rename.

findings.title: action.code maximum cardinality decreased from 0..* to 0..1

oldState.summary: R4 allowed multiple CodeableConcept codes per action.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 action could carry more than one `code` element to classify or describe the action.

newState.summary: R6 allows at most one CodeableConcept code per action.

binding.description: Provides examples of actions to be performed.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 narrows each action to a single CodeableConcept, though that CodeableConcept can still contain multiple codings for the same concept.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is a direct validation break for any R4 action with two or more `code` repetitions. Runtime risk is moderate because systems that stored multiple independent classifications must choose a representation strategy.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that action.code is one classification concept rather than a repeatable list of concepts.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `action.code` repeatable and use definition, warning, profile, or implementation-guide guidance to prefer a single CodeableConcept when appropriate.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: A cleaner single-classification model is a reasonable inferred goal, especially because one `CodeableConcept` can carry multiple codings for the same concept. However, decreasing max cardinality from `*` to `1` directly invalidates R4 actions with multiple code repetitions, and the supplied definitions do not show why base validation had to enforce that immediately. Keeping the repeatable element with stronger guidance would preserve R4 content with modest tradeoff, so the hard break was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design would retain `action.code` at `0..*`, clarify that alternate codings for the same classification should normally be carried in one `CodeableConcept`, and let profiles or warning rules require `0..1` where interoperability needs that constraint. This preserves legacy instances while still communicating the preferred R6 modeling pattern.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Base R6 would still allow unusual repeated classifications, but CodeableConcept already supports multiple codings and stricter profiles can enforce one concept.

evidence.detail: R4 max cardinality is `*`.
R6 max cardinality is `1`.
R6 adds an example binding for action code examples.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is intentionally lossy-looking: independent CodeableConcept repetitions may not safely collapse into one concept without domain review. Multiple codings for the same concept can usually be merged into one CodeableConcept.

findings.narrativeMd: The `action.code` repeatability reduction is a classic hard instance-breaking change. R4 authors could attach several CodeableConcept classifications to an action; R6 permits only one. This affects validators immediately and affects business logic that filtered, ranked, or grouped actions using multiple code repetitions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 action with multiple `code` repetitions can be invalid in R6 because it violates `max=1`. R6-to-R4 is not a problem for this field because one code is allowed in R4. The migration problem is semantic: multiple old concepts may not have a single equivalent R6 CodeableConcept.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory actions with more than one `code`. If repeated codings express the same concept in different systems, merge them into one CodeableConcept. If they express distinct classifications, choose a primary code and move secondary classifications to extensions, profiles, or downstream metadata with human review.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change could have been avoided by keeping `0..*`; however, if the intent is to ensure `code` is a single action classification, a base cardinality change is the strongest enforcement mechanism. A warning invariant would have been less disruptive but less interoperable.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `PlanDefinition.action.code` changed from repeatable to single-valued. That is a direct validation break for R4 actions that used multiple CodeableConcepts to classify an action. Some repeated codings can be collapsed into one CodeableConcept, but distinct classifications require a primary/secondary decision or an extension, which is expert-dependent and potentially changes filtering or grouping behavior.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.code` has cardinality 0..* and type `CodeableConcept`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.code` has cardinality 0..1 and type `CodeableConcept`.
R6 keeps only an example binding, so the material change is cardinality rather than terminology strength.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 2/trial-use does not create a high stability burden by itself, but the path-level narrowing and potentially lossy consolidation drive the judgment.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: any R4 action with two or more `code` repetitions violates R6 `max=1`; migration may also lose meaning when repetitions are distinct concepts.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes: keep `action.code` at 0..* in the base resource and use definition text, warnings, profiles, or IG rules to prefer one conceptual CodeableConcept. This preserves old instances with modest cost.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing hard-break and less-breaking-alternative-available assessment, even though prevalence remains uncertain.

findings.title: action.timing[x] removed dateTime and Period choices and added RelativeTime

oldState.summary: R4 choices: dateTime, Age, Period, Duration, Range, Timing.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 could express action timing directly as an absolute `timingDateTime` or as a `timingPeriod`, in addition to relative and repeated timing datatypes.

newState.summary: R6 choices: Age, Duration, Range, Timing, RelativeTime.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 removes the direct `dateTime` and `Period` choices and adds `RelativeTime`. Absolute dates or periods must be represented using another allowed type, usually `Timing`, if possible.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances using `timingDateTime` or `timingPeriod` are not valid against the R6 choice set. R6 instances using `timingRelativeTime` cannot be represented in R4 without an extension or approximate conversion.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Timing governs when planned actions occur. Incorrect conversion can change clinical or operational scheduling.

justification.inferredGoal: Favor relative and schedulable timing forms and introduce RelativeTime.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Add `RelativeTime` while retaining `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod` as deprecated or warning-only legacy choices.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 comment explains `timing[x]` as a definitional instruction evaluated during apply, which supports favoring Age, Duration, Range, Timing, and RelativeTime over bare absolute date/time and Period choices. Retaining the legacy choices would reduce migration breakage, but it would keep ambiguous timing forms alive and duplicate concepts that can often be represented through `Timing.event` or `Timing.repeat.boundsPeriod`. Those material semantic and safety tradeoffs make the break probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would add `RelativeTime` and keep `dateTime` and `Period` as deprecated or warning-producing choices. This would preserve R4 instances using `timingDateTime` or `timingPeriod`, but it is only a partial alternative because processors would still need to interpret several overlapping timing forms in a definitional apply context.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves old wire names but leaves multiple timing representations and perpetuates absolute or period forms that can be ambiguous in definitional apply-time semantics.

evidence.detail: R4 includes dateTime and Period choices.
R6 excludes dateTime and Period and includes RelativeTime.

examples.examplesMd: The `RelativeTime` example is schematic because the full RelativeTime datatype should be validated in its own datatype report.

findings.narrativeMd: The R6 choice set for action timing is not a pure widening. It removes two R4 wire names, `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod`, so existing instances using them need an explicit transform. The addition of `RelativeTime` also creates a new timing representation that R4 systems will not understand.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod` elements are old-valid/new-invalid at the PlanDefinition level. Some values can be converted to `timingTiming`, but conversion should be tested because a direct choice element becomes a nested datatype representation. R6 `timingRelativeTime` is not R4-representable without extension or loss of precision.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map absolute dateTime values to `Timing.event` where that preserves intent. Map Period values to `Timing.repeat.boundsPeriod` when appropriate. Treat `RelativeTime` as an R6-only feature for R4 conversion unless a project-specific extension or approximation is defined. Include action scheduling tests around point-in-time, interval, repeat, and relative cases.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Keeping dateTime and Period while adding RelativeTime would have been the least disruptive path. If R6 intended to reduce ambiguous timing forms, removal gives stronger consistency but shifts conversion burden to implementers.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 removes the direct `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod` choices while adding `RelativeTime`. R4 instances using those removed choice names require transformation, and R6 `RelativeTime` cannot be represented in base R4 without an extension or approximation. For forward migration, however, the removed R4 cases have natural R6 `Timing` encodings (`Timing.event` and `Timing.repeat.boundsPeriod`), and the R6 model appears to favor schedulable or relative timing forms for a reusable definition.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.timing[x]` includes `dateTime`, `Age`, `Period`, `Duration`, `Range`, and `Timing`.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.timing[x]` includes `Age`, `Duration`, `Range`, `Timing`, and `RelativeTime`.
The affected path is an action scheduling field, so transforms should be tested rather than silently dropped.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral; it keeps attention on the concrete scheduling mechanism and on whether the old choices are reasonably transformable.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 `timingDateTime` and `timingPeriod` choice names are outside the R6 choice set; R6-to-R4 loss exists for `timingRelativeTime`.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial: R6 could have retained `dateTime` and `Period` as deprecated choices while adding `RelativeTime`, but that would leave overlapping timing representations that duplicate `Timing.event` and `Timing.repeat.boundsPeriod` in a definitional apply context.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact and partial-alternative assessment; I agree the break is real but judge the design proportionate because old forward cases can usually be transformed into `Timing`.

findings.title: Action participant model expanded and required participant-type codes changed

oldState.summary: R4 participant.type was mandatory and bound to four required codes.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: Local CodeSystem concepts were compared; no terminology server expansion was performed.

oldState.narrativeMd: R4 required every participant to carry a primitive participant type code such as `patient`, `practitioner`, `related-person`, or `device`.

newState.summary: R6 participant.type is optional, the code set is expanded/renamed, and actor/canonical/reference alternatives are available.

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: R6 replaces the R4 hyphenated `related-person` code with `relatedperson` and adds several participant categories.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds a top-level `actor` backbone and allows action participants to reference an actor (`actorId`), define the participant by canonical/reference type, and specify a `function`. The primitive `type` code is no longer required but still uses a required binding when present.

facts.note: Appears to be a spelling/identifier normalization, but no ConceptMap was supplied.

impact.impactRationaleMd: An R4 participant using the required code `related-person` is invalid under the R6 required code system, which uses `relatedperson`. R6 participants may also omit `type` and instead use actor/canonical/reference forms that have no R4 equivalent.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Performer and participant semantics can affect task assignment, care-team routing, and generated requests.

justification.inferredGoal: Support richer participant definitions and align participant categories with more resource types and definitional actors.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain `related-person` as a deprecated alias for `relatedperson` while adding the broader actor, canonical, reference, and function fields.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The richer R6 participant and actor model is reasonable, and most of it is additive or a cardinality relaxation for R4-to-R6. The hard forward break is mainly the removal of the required-bound R4 code `related-person`. A base R6 value set could have accepted that spelling as deprecated while also adding `relatedperson` and the new actor fields, so the code-spelling break was probably avoidable.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The less-breaking base design would include both `related-person` and `relatedperson` in the required participant-type code system/value set, with deprecation and normalization guidance for the old spelling. ConceptMaps and conversion notes are useful migration aids, but the base-design alternative is to keep the old code valid. R6-only actor-based participants would still need down-conversion policy for R4, but that is a separate R6-to-R4 issue.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Creates two spellings for the RelatedPerson concept and a normalization burden, but preserves R4 instances without blocking the R6 actor model.

evidence.detail: R4 participant.type is 1..1 code with required action-participant-type binding.
R6 participant.type is 0..1 code with required action-participant-type binding.
R6 adds top-level actor definitions.
R6 participants can reference a PlanDefinition actor by id.
R4 local CodeSystem includes `related-person`; R6 local CodeSystem includes `relatedperson` and does not include `related-person`.

examples.examplesMd: The apparent R4-to-R6 code mapping `related-person` to `relatedperson` should be confirmed with official cross-version terminology guidance before automated production use.

findings.narrativeMd: Participant modeling changed in both syntax and terminology. The old required participant type code is now optional because R6 can identify participants through actors and references, but when the code is used it draws from a changed required code system. The most visible old-valid/new-invalid case is `related-person`, which becomes `relatedperson` in R6.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `participant.type = related-person` fail R6 required-binding validation. Other R4 codes such as `patient`, `practitioner`, and `device` remain present in the local R6 CodeSystem. R6 actor-based or reference-based participants do not fit the R4 participant shape without flattening and information loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map known old participant codes to R6 codes, especially `related-person` to `relatedperson`, but treat that as a terminology migration requiring review because no local ConceptMap was found. For R6 actor-based participants, decide whether to inline an approximate R4 `type`, preserve actor details in extensions, or block down-conversion.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The actor model is a reasonable structural enhancement, but the required code spelling change could have been softened by retaining aliases or publishing a ConceptMap. Without that, implementations must hard-code cross-version terminology logic.

freshReview.narrativeMd: Most of the R6 participant model is additive or relaxing for R4-to-R6 migration: `participant.type` becomes optional, top-level actors are added, and canonical/reference/function alternatives increase expressivity. The hard forward break is the required-bound code spelling change from `related-person` to `relatedperson`. An R4 participant using the old valid code becomes invalid under the R6 required binding even though the concept is the same RelatedPerson role.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.participant.type` is 1..1 `code` with required action-participant-type binding.
R6 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.action.participant.type` is 0..1 `code` with required action-participant-type binding, with actor/canonical/reference alternatives added.
R4 CodeSystem action-participant-type includes `related-person`; R6 CodeSystem includes `relatedperson` and not `related-person`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral; the Revisit judgment comes from the avoidable required-code removal, not from a mature-artifact stability presumption.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 `participant.type = related-person` fails the R6 required code set; R6-to-R4 loss also exists for actor-based participants.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Yes: include `related-person` as a deprecated alias while adding `relatedperson` and the richer actor model. The tradeoff is a normalization burden and two spellings for one concept, but it preserves R4 instances without blocking the new model.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing high-impact and less-breaking-alternative-available assessment for the terminology break; the actor additions are useful but do not justify removing the old code from the required set.

findings.title: R6 widens subject, action definition, and goal target detail domains beyond R4

oldState.summary: R4 subject and definition choices had narrower target/type sets; goal target detail allowed Quantity, Range, or CodeableConcept.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 PlanDefinition subject references were limited to Group, action definitions targeted ActivityDefinition/PlanDefinition/Questionnaire or URI, and goal target details were limited to Quantity, Range, or CodeableConcept.

newState.summary: R6 adds canonical subjects, product-definition subject targets, more action definition targets, and scalar/Ratio goal target details.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 can target additional definitional resources from `subject[x]`, can use canonical subject forms, can point action definitions at Measure, MessageDefinition, ObservationDefinition, OperationDefinition, and SpecimenDefinition, and can express goal target details as string/boolean/integer/Ratio.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These are mostly widenings, so ordinary R4 instances remain valid on these dimensions. The risk is down-conversion and generated model coverage: R6 instances can use choice names and canonical/reference targets that R4 PlanDefinition cannot express.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Subject and definition targets can determine which population or artifact an executable plan applies to. Dropping them can change applicability.

justification.inferredGoal: Extend PlanDefinition beyond clinical-care-only subjects and allow additional definitional artifacts as action definitions and goal details.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 base alternative is needed because these subject, definition, and goal-detail domains are widened while retaining the R4 forms.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: These changes add R6 expressivity without invalidating R4 instances that use the shared subject, definition, or goal target detail forms. The compatibility issue is downstream and reverse-direction: valid R6 content may not fit into R4. Under the calibration rules, that makes the backward-compatible-alternative question not applicable for the R4-to-R6 base design, and the additive widening is justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Extensions, external metadata, or explicit rejection may be needed when exporting R6-only choices such as `subjectCanonical` or `detailRatio` to R4. Those are R6-to-R4 mitigation strategies, not alternatives to a breaking R6 base design, because the R6 base model already preserves the R4-valid shapes.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-only choices and targets need extension mapping or rejection for R6-to-R4 conversion, but that is not a less-breaking base R6 design alternative.

evidence.detail: R4 subject choices are CodeableConcept or Reference(Group).
R6 subject adds canonical(EvidenceVariable) and additional product/substance reference targets.
R4 action.definition canonical targets ActivityDefinition, PlanDefinition, and Questionnaire.
R6 action.definition adds Measure, MessageDefinition, ObservationDefinition, OperationDefinition, and SpecimenDefinition targets.
R6 goal target detail adds string, boolean, integer, and Ratio.

examples.examplesMd: This is an R6-only expressivity example; R4 has no `subjectCanonical`, `detailRatio`, or Measure target for action.definition.

findings.narrativeMd: Several R6 choice and reference domains are widened. These are not R4-to-R6 validation breaks, but they matter for cross-version services because valid R6 plans can now identify subjects and definitions that R4 clients do not model and can express goal target details with new primitive or Ratio choices.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 content remains valid for the shared choices. R6 content using the new choices is not cleanly R4-representable: choice element names differ, target profiles are outside R4's declared domain, and strict R4 validators/code generators will reject or ignore them.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 conversion, detect these R6-only choices and either preserve them in extensions, map them to project-specific R4 profiles, or reject down-conversion. For R4-to-R6, no transform is needed for existing shared choices, but applications should update model classes and FHIRPath to handle the new choice names.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: These widenings appear to reflect real new scope in R6. R4 cannot express them without extensions, so a fully backward-compatible base representation was not available once the new domains were accepted.

freshReview.narrativeMd: This finding is mainly a set of R6 widenings: added subject choices/targets, added action definition targets, and added goal target detail datatypes. The R4 shapes remain available, so existing R4 instances do not become invalid on these paths. A converter exporting newer R6 content back to R4 needs policy for the new choices, but that reverse-direction limitation is inherent in adding expressivity and does not indicate a problematic R6 base design.
keyEvidence: R4 `PlanDefinition.subject[x]` supports CodeableConcept and Reference(Group); R6 adds canonical(EvidenceVariable) and product/substance-related reference targets.

R4 `PlanDefinition.action.definition[x]` targets ActivityDefinition, PlanDefinition, and Questionnaire; R6 adds Measure, MessageDefinition, ObservationDefinition, OperationDefinition, and SpecimenDefinition targets.
R6 `PlanDefinition.goal.target.detail[x]` adds string, boolean, integer, and Ratio while retaining the R4-compatible forms.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use did not amplify this because there is no forward compatibility break; additive widening is acceptable under this maturity level.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: R6-only choices and targets cannot be represented in base R4, but there is no old-valid/new-invalid R4-to-R6 mechanism.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable: R6 retained the R4-valid forms and only widened the domains. Extensions or rejection policies for down-conversion are migration mitigations, not less-breaking base R6 designs.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing representability-risk observation, but disagree that this should be treated as a material breaking-change concern; it is reverse-only additive expressivity.

findings.title: Several text fields changed primitive type from string to markdown

oldState.summary: R4 modeled these fields as primitive string.
oldState.narrativeMd: `usage`, `action.description`, and `action.textEquivalent` were simple strings in R4.

newState.summary: R6 models these fields as primitive markdown.
newState.narrativeMd: The same JSON member names remain, but their FHIR primitive type is now `markdown`, which can carry formatting semantics and may map to a distinct generated type.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The wire member names are unchanged and ordinary JSON string values are likely to parse, but generated classes, primitive validators, renderers, and sanitizers may treat markdown differently from string.

justification.inferredGoal: Allow formatted narrative text in usage and action descriptions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the fields typed as `string` and state in definitions or guidance that markdown syntax may be used.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The affected fields are human-facing prose, so the R6 goal of explicit markdown semantics is reasonable. Ordinary JSON string values are still wire-compatible, but generated models, primitive validators, renderers, and sanitizers can see a real type change. Keeping `string` with prose guidance would be less disruptive, but it would only partially meet the goal because conformance tooling would not know that markdown semantics are intended. The change is therefore probably justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would retain the R4 `string` primitive for `usage`, `action.description`, and `action.textEquivalent`, while strengthening comments or guidance to allow markdown content. This preserves R4-era generated types but relies on prose rather than a computable primitive type, leaving weaker support for safe markdown rendering and validation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids generated primitive-type churn but loses the computable markdown signal for validation, rendering, and sanitization.

evidence.detail: R4 usage type is string.
R6 usage type is markdown.
R4 action.description type is string.
R6 action.description type is markdown.
R4 action.textEquivalent type is string.
R6 action.textEquivalent type is markdown.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 example is syntactically a JSON string and can be stored in R4, but R4 systems may not interpret or sanitize it as markdown.

findings.narrativeMd: This is not a typical hard validation break because FHIR JSON still carries primitive markdown as a string value. It is nevertheless relevant for code generation and runtime rendering: R4 applications may have treated these fields as inert plain text, while R6 applications may render markdown or apply markdown-specific validation and sanitization.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Plain R4 strings should generally remain acceptable as R6 markdown values, so old-valid/new-invalid risk is low. The main compatibility issue is behavioral: typed SDKs may expose a different primitive class, and UIs must avoid unsafe markdown rendering assumptions. R6 markdown content can be copied into R4 string fields but may lose declared formatting semantics.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update generated models and serializers for the primitive type change. Review UI rendering and sanitization paths. If down-converting to R4, either preserve markdown as literal text or strip/escape formatting according to local display policy.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Using markdown directly is more expressive and consistent with other FHIR narrative fields. A string-plus-guidance approach would reduce codegen churn but would hide formatting expectations from conformance tooling.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `usage`, `action.description`, and `action.textEquivalent` changed from FHIR `string` to FHIR `markdown`, but the JSON member names and primitive wire representation remain string values. Typed SDKs, renderers, and sanitizers may need to recognize markdown semantics, yet ordinary R4 string payloads are not made invalid by this change. The main risk is local display policy, not a base compatibility break.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition: `PlanDefinition.usage`, `PlanDefinition.action.description`, and `PlanDefinition.action.textEquivalent` are type `string`.
R6 StructureDefinition: the same three paths are type `markdown` with unchanged element names.
FHIR JSON serializes both primitives as JSON strings, with any primitive extensions still carried through the same underscore companion pattern.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral; because the wire shape stays compatible, maturity did not push this beyond migration awareness.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: generated primitive classes or UI rendering behavior can change, but there is no ordinary old-valid/new-invalid instance break.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Partial but unnecessary: keeping `string` with prose guidance would reduce primitive-type churn, but it would hide the computable markdown signal needed by validators and safe renderers.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that codegen/runtime awareness is useful, but disagree with treating the impact as more than low practical concern because the wire value remains a string.

findings.title: R6 adds local warning invariants for canonical hygiene, goal/action references, and relatedArtifact use

oldState.summary: R4 had the PlanDefinition-specific `pdf-0` name warning plus inherited resource constraints.

constraints.human: Name should be usable as an identifier for the module by machine processing applications such as code generation

oldState.narrativeMd: The local R4 PlanDefinition warning checked name shape, but allowed a single uppercase letter and did not add PlanDefinition-specific warnings for goal/action target resolution or relatedArtifact type usage.

newState.summary: R6 has stricter canonical-name/url warnings and new PlanDefinition-specific relationship warnings.

constraints.human: Name should be usable as an identifier for the module by machine processing applications such as code generation
URL should not contain | or # - these characters make processing canonical references problematic
goalid should reference the id of a goal definition
targetId should reference the id of an action

constraints.expression: type in ('depends-on' | 'part-of') implies ((resource.exists() xor resourceReference.exists()) or (artifact is canonical xor artifact is Reference))
constraints.human: Dependencies of a PlanDefinition should reference a resource

newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds several warning-level checks that can affect conformance dashboards and CI pipelines even though they are not error-level base validation failures.

facts.newValue: cnl-0 requires at least two characters when name exists
cnl-1 url should not contain |, #, or space
pld-3 goalId should resolve to goal.id
pld-4 targetId should resolve to action.id
pld-6 dependencies should reference a resource
pld-7 PlanDefinition should not have relatedArtifact.type composed-of

impact.impactRationaleMd: All listed constraints are warning-level, so they do not create hard invalid instances under normal FHIR validation. They can still break pipelines that treat warnings as failures or rely on warning-free conformance for publication.

justification.inferredGoal: Improve canonical hygiene and catch broken internal PlanDefinition references or inappropriate dependency modeling.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking base alternative is needed because R6 introduced these checks as warning-severity constraints rather than errors.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The new constraints address legitimate quality issues: canonical hygiene, internal goal/action references, and relatedArtifact use. Because they are warning-level constraints, the R6 base design does not make R4 content structurally invalid under normal validation severity handling. The compatibility-preserving base approach is already used, so the alternative question is not applicable and the change is justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Suppressing the warnings or moving them only to external guidance would reduce conformance noise, but it would also weaken generic QA. Treating warnings as fatal is an implementation or publication-policy choice, not a base R6 design break that requires a backward-compatible alternative.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Existing artifacts may produce new warnings, but hard failures come from local tooling or publication policy that escalates warnings.

evidence.detail: R4 has pdf-0 name warning.
R6 root has cnl-0, pld-3, and pld-4 warnings.
R6 url has canonical hygiene warning cnl-1.
R6 relatedArtifact has new PlanDefinition-specific warnings.

examples.examplesMd: A PlanDefinition named `A`, a URL containing `#`, an unresolved `goalId`, or a `relatedArtifact.type` of `composed-of` may still be structurally valid but warning-producing in R6.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 tightens local conformance expectations through warnings rather than errors. These changes are easy to miss because they do not alter cardinality or type, but they can affect artifact publication, quality gates, and automated code generation policies that require warning-free canonical resources.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Under standard severity handling these are not hard breaking: R4-valid content becomes R6-valid-with-warnings rather than invalid. Environments that escalate warnings can experience operational breaks. The stricter `cnl-0` name pattern also means a one-character uppercase name that satisfied R4 `pdf-0` no longer satisfies the R6 warning expression.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Run R6 validation and triage warning output. Normalize canonical URLs, ensure `goalId` and `targetId` values resolve internally, avoid `relatedArtifact.type = composed-of` on PlanDefinition, and review dependency relatedArtifact representations. Decide explicitly whether migration tooling treats these warnings as blocking.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Warnings are a relatively backward-compatible way to introduce stricter expectations. The avoidable part is warning churn for existing artifacts, but the severity choice avoids making old instances structurally invalid.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The added R6 constraints are warning-level checks for canonical hygiene, internal goal/action references, and relatedArtifact usage. They can create new QA findings or fail a local pipeline that treats warnings as fatal, but the base StructureDefinition does not turn matching R4 content into an error-level invalid instance. This is the compatibility-preserving way to introduce stronger guidance.
keyEvidence: R4 root constraint includes the local `pdf-0` name warning.
R6 root and URL constraints include warning-level `cnl-0`, `cnl-1`, `pld-3`, and `pld-4`.
R6 `PlanDefinition.relatedArtifact` adds warning-level `pld-6` and `pld-7`.
All material local constraints in this finding are severity `warning`, not `error`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use is neutral; warning severity keeps the change below a material base-breaking threshold.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: warning-level: R4-era content may produce new R6 warnings, especially in warning-as-error publication pipelines, but remains structurally valid under normal severity handling.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable: warning-level invariants are already the less-breaking alternative to hard cardinality, type, or error-level constraints. Prose-only guidance would be weaker but not meaningfully more compatible at the base-validation level.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing warning-level mechanism, but disagree with elevating it to a medium breaking concern; local warning escalation is an implementation policy.

findings.title: R6 adds optional metadata and behavior elements with no base R4 representation

oldState.summary: R4 has no corresponding base elements for these R6 fields.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 lacks explicit version comparison algorithm, copyright label, plan-level as-needed precondition, action linkId, action location, and action applicability behavior elements.

newState.summary: R6 adds optional elements for version sorting, labels, preconditions, action linkage, location, and child-action applicability behavior.

binding.description: Defines applicability behavior of a group.

newState.narrativeMd: The new fields are optional for R4-to-R6 migration, but a valid R6 PlanDefinition can depend on them for version ordering, display/legal labeling, as-needed preconditions, realization linkage, location, and child-action applicability behavior.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Optional additions do not invalidate R4 instances migrating forward. They do create down-conversion risk because R4 has no standard element for these semantics, and some of them affect execution behavior.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: `action.location`, `asNeeded[x]`, and `applicabilityBehavior` can influence where, when, and whether planned actions apply.

justification.inferredGoal: Add explicit support for common publication metadata and action orchestration semantics.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No R4-to-R6 alternative is needed because these are optional additive R6 elements and do not invalidate R4 instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: `versionAlgorithm[x]`, `copyrightLabel`, `asNeeded[x]`, `action.linkId`, `action.location`, and `action.applicabilityBehavior` add useful optional metadata and action semantics. Since R4 instances can omit all of them and still migrate forward, this is not a breaking R4-to-R6 base-design issue. The additive design is justified.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For R6-to-R4 export, projects may need extensions, external metadata, or explicit loss/rejection policies for these new fields. Those are appropriate migration mitigations, but they are not backward-compatible base R6 alternatives because the R6 base model already chose the compatibility-preserving additive shape.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: R6-to-R4 preservation requires extensions or conversion policy, which is down-conversion mitigation rather than a base R6 alternative.

evidence.detail: R6 adds versionAlgorithm[x] with string and Coding choices.
R6 adds copyrightLabel.
R6 adds asNeeded[x] with boolean and CodeableConcept choices.
R6 adds action.linkId.
R6 adds action.location as CodeableReference(Location).
R6 adds action.applicabilityBehavior with required all/any binding.

examples.examplesMd: R4 can preserve these only through extensions or external metadata, not through standard PlanDefinition elements.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 adds several optional elements that are safe for forward validation but important for round-trip conversion. Because these elements are semantically meaningful, simply dropping them in R6-to-R4 transforms can alter version ordering, legal display, action applicability, action realization linkage, or location-specific execution guidance.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances are not invalidated by these additions. Valid R6 instances using them are not base-R4-representable without extensions or external metadata. Strict R4 parsers will reject the unknown elements if they appear directly in R4-shaped JSON.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R4-to-R6, no default population is required. For R6-to-R4, define extensions for fields that must survive, and document any fields intentionally dropped. Pay special attention to `applicabilityBehavior` and `location` because they may affect execution semantics rather than only publication metadata.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Optional additions are the most compatible way to add R6 features. The remaining incompatibility is inherent to trying to represent newer R6 semantics in the older R4 base resource.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The listed R6 elements are optional additions: version algorithm, copyright label, plan-level as-needed, action linkId, action location, and applicability behavior. They do not invalidate any R4 PlanDefinition moving forward. Some have real execution or publication semantics, so R6-to-R4 exporters should preserve them in extensions or reject lossy conversion when needed, but that is a normal consequence of optional new R6 expressivity.
keyEvidence: R6 StructureDefinition adds optional `PlanDefinition.versionAlgorithm[x]`, `copyrightLabel`, and `asNeeded[x]`.
R6 StructureDefinition adds optional `PlanDefinition.action.linkId`, `action.location`, and `action.applicabilityBehavior`.
No corresponding required R6 element is introduced for existing R4 instances to populate.
freshReview.fmmEffect: FMM 2/trial-use did not increase concern because the changes are additive and optional for R4-to-R6 migration.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: direct base-R4 representation is missing for the new optional fields, but there is no R4-to-R6 invalidation mechanism.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: Not applicable: adding optional base elements is already the compatibility-preserving design. R4 extensions or external metadata are down-conversion mitigations, not less-breaking R6 base alternatives.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing R6-to-R4 representability warning, but disagree that this is a breaking-design problem because the additions are optional and forward-compatible.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: R6 PlanDefinition exists at the same canonical URL, resource type, kind, baseDefinition, and derivation as R4. The resource was not renamed, split, merged, abstracted, or removed.

All local min/max changes were reviewed. The material changes are reported for `action.code` and `action.participant.type`; no other local PlanDefinition element had a material cardinality narrowing. Optional R6 additions are covered as representability risks.

Required local action behavior/status/priority/condition/relationship code systems available in the packages were compared and showed no material code removals except participant type. Some extensible/preferred/example bindings moved to terminology.hl7.org value sets not present locally, so expansion-level comparison was limited.
No local reference target narrowing was found. R6 target/domain widenings for subject and action.definition are reported as R6-to-R4 representability risks.
The local `PlanDefinition.status` modifier flag remains true. No local element gained or lost modifier status. Inherited modifierExtension details are out of scope.
No local summary-flag change was identified as material for PlanDefinition. The observed `modifierExtension` summary-flag difference is inherited/base-artifact scope and excluded.
No material local slicing changes were found in the PlanDefinition snapshot/differential comparison.
No local fixed value, pattern, or default value changes were found for PlanDefinition elements.
No local maxLength, minValue, maxValue, or regex constraints besides the warning-level name/url invariants were found.
Serialization/codegen-relevant changes were found and reported for input/output wrappers, renamed relatedAction fields, choice-type changes, and string-to-markdown primitive changes.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: PlanDefinition StructureDefinition status changed from draft to active
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: This is metadata about the definition artifact, not an instance element constraint. It does not make R4 PlanDefinition instances invalid in R6.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Treat R6 ballot maturity/status as relevant for governance, but not as an instance transform requirement.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: R6 snapshot explicitly carries mustSupport=false on many elements
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R4 generally omitted `mustSupport`; R6 explicitly setting false does not require instances to populate those elements and does not create a local Must Support obligation.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Generated metadata differs, but this should not be treated as a new conformance requirement unless a profile overrides it.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Several non-required bindings moved to terminology.hl7.org canonical value sets
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The affected bindings are extensible, preferred, or example in the base resource, so they do not create the same hard validation behavior as required bindings.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology resolution configuration may need updates, especially because some referenced terminology.hl7.org value sets were not present in the local R6 core package.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: PlanDefinition action input/output migration depends on preserving nested DataRequirement content. Any R4-to-R6 changes inside DataRequirement itself should be applied after the wrapper transform.
R6 adds `RelativeTime` to `action.timing[x]`. Its datatype-specific compatibility and possible R4 extension strategy should be assessed separately.
R6 adds `action.location` as CodeableReference(Location). Down-conversion policy depends on CodeableReference representation and datatype compatibility.
R6 adds PlanDefinition-specific warnings involving RelatedArtifact fields such as resource/resourceReference/artifact. Changes inside RelatedArtifact should be assessed in that datatype's report.
Inherited/base-artifact changes, including inherited extension/modifierExtension details, were intentionally excluded from this local PlanDefinition report under the assignment scope rule.
A ConceptMap or official terminology migration guide would confirm participant-type code mappings and value set URL moves.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official HL7 R4-to-R6 diff or ballot change notes were available in the supplied inputs, so rationale and avoidability assessments are inferred from StructureDefinition deltas.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Provide the official PlanDefinition diff/changelog or rendered specification change notes.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Local CodeSystems were compared where present, but no terminology server expansion was performed. Several R6 bindings point to terminology.hl7.org value sets that were not present in the local core package.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Run terminology expansions for all bound value sets and review official cross-version ConceptMaps.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No PlanDefinition example resources were found in either local core package, so prevalence estimates are based on model semantics rather than package examples.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review implementation guides, production instances, or HL7 example repositories containing PlanDefinition instances.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The new artifact is an R6 ballot build. Findings reflect the supplied 6.0.0-ballot4 package and could change before final publication.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Re-run the comparison against the final published R6 package.

suggestedMigrationBacklogGroups: PlanDefinition participant and actor terminology migration
crossArtifactPatternsToCheck: Action input/output DataRequirement wrapper changes across RequestOrchestration and related workflow artifacts
relatedAction actionId/targetId rename across action-based resources
Timing choice removal/addition patterns involving RelativeTime
